references.text: God creates living creatures in the sea according to their kinds, parallel to the creation of land animals according to their kinds in verse 25.
God's command that the earth should bring forth living creatures according to their kind - verse 25 is the fulfillment of this command.
God forms all the beasts of the field and the birds of the heavens from the ground, expanding on the creation account from chapter 1.
The animals are to come to the ark 'according to their kinds' - the same terminology used in creation, where God arranged the animals according to their kinds.
Job urges people to ask the animals and the birds, all of whom testify that God's hand has created everything living.
The psalmist praises God's many works of creation and the wisdom behind the diversity of creatures on earth.
God declares that He has created the earth with the humans and animals upon it by His great power.
Both verses illustrate God's ordering of creation by creating each kind 'according to its kind' and confirming that this is 'good'.
Both verses use the phrase 'each according to its kind' to describe God's ordering of life, first for plants (1:11) and then for animals (1:25).
Genesis 1:31 summarizes the creation of the animals from 1:25 as part of the whole that God saw was 'very good'.
Noah's instruction to let the animals go out so they may multiply is a restoration of the original creation order described in 1:25.
Paul uses the creation principle from 1:25 ('each according to its kind') as an analogy for how God gives each creature its own body in the resurrection.
The verses create a strong contrast between the original good creation of the animals and the later corruption of all flesh.
Entering the ark confirms that the created order from 1:25 was preserved by taking 'all kinds' of animals according to their kinds.
God's remembrance of the animals in the ark is a direct result of His creative act described in 1:25, highlighting His faithfulness.
The psalm uses the list of animals from the creation account (Gen 1:25) to illustrate humanity's dominion over creation.
